title: A First Day of School Activity that Teaches Argumentation
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart describes the activity he plans to open the school year with: every student brainstorms five or so clear, precise, arguable claims that tell the class something true about them. The move is to fuse the standard get-to-know-you icebreaker with the first lesson in argumentation so that Day 1 does double duty. He grounds the choice in the previous year's experience rather than in Common Core enthusiasm - his students arrived with little argumentative know-how, and argumentation turned out to be the lens through which many of them began flourishing as intellectuals. He models the move first with his own life, converting facts about his family, faith, tacos and a hated pop song into claims someone could argue with, then asks the class to judge thumbs up or down whether each is genuinely debatable and uses index cards to draft students into producing counterclaims. Students then draft their own claims, get triad feedback on which one to read, and read a single claim to the whole class. His stated goals expose the belief underneath the activity: an argument is not about winning but about getting to the bottom of things, so the icebreaker teaches a disposition as much as a skill.
points: The design principle is that Day 1 should be academically real - the icebreaker is also the year's first lesson in claim-making, so no instructional day is spent purely on rapport.
Stuart models with his own life first, turning 'I like tacos' into a claim someone could contest, which shows students concretely what makes a statement arguable rather than merely true.
The thumbs-up/thumbs-down check plus index-card cold calls for counterclaims turns a light activity into a formative read on whether students can distinguish a claim from a fact.
Triad rehearsal before whole-class sharing lowers the cost of the first public speaking moment of the year, since peers help each student choose which claim to read aloud.
He justifies argument as the lens through which his weakest students began flourishing intellectually, which is why he spends opening-day time on it rather than on procedures.
quotes: In our school, we have to set goals for ourselves that can be measured with data. My goals are focused around W.CCR.1 and R.CCR.10 — writing argumentatively from a variety of complex texts. This is not because I'm a Common Core baller; rather, it's because, during CCSS-ish experimenting with my courses last year, I found that students had little argumentative know-how and that argumentation was a lens through which so many of them began flourishing as intellectuals.

So anyways, here's the hotness: to help me get to know my students, and to introduce them to the awesomeness of argumentation on the first day, I'm going to have each student brainstorm five or so clear and precise arguable claims that tell the rest of the class something about them. I'll begin by modeling something like this:
Now, how can I turn these into debatable claims? In other words, how can I state them in a way that you could argue with me?

After I share each arguable claim, I will ask students to give me a thumbs up or thumbs down on whether it is debatable. I will then use index cards to call on students and ask them to make a counterclaim. Once I've modeled this and a few students have successfully done it, I'll ask them to go to work writing their own claims that tell us something about them.

After five minutes or so, I'll have them share all of their draft claims in their triads, and I'll ask triad-mates to help each member choose which claim they should read to the whole class. Finally, each student will read a claim to the whole class, and we'll do some mad clapping, and we'll move on.
Begin demonstrating the collaborative, creative, and awesome nature of arguments. The point of an argument isn't winning, but rather it's getting to the bottom of things.
